Author

About this report

This report summarizes the result of experiments on applying ensemble learning to classifiy Zika news articles pipeline outputs. The report is organized into three main sections corresponding to the three stages of the pipeline:

  1. Google News retrieval and cached manifest status
  2. Headline ensemble filtering diagnostics using cloud OpenAI (gpt-5-nano) and local DeepSeek (deepseek-r1:14b) models
  3. Full-text retrieval status

Step 1 Retrieval

Note

The manifest currently spans 2010-01-01 to 2025-12-31.

Stage 1 is implemented with a two-step workflow:

  1. Network retrieval builds daily Google News search windows, checks the manifest, queries only unfinished windows, and writes one cached JSON payload per window.
  2. Parsing and normalization re-reads cached payloads with status %in% c("success", "empty"), flattens the feed entries into a table, and applies deterministic deduplication before writing the final CSV and Parquet outputs.

The retrieval script is therefore optimized for interruption and restart, while the parsing script is optimized for fast reruns from cache.

How the retrieval step works

  1. Build daily windows from the configured query period.
  2. Use the manifest as the authoritative checkpoint to decide whether a window is already complete, due for retry, or still pending.
  3. Query Google News using the English / US edition configuration and persist the raw JSON payload to zika/data/raw/rss/.
  4. Detect throttling from HTTP status and Google “Sorry” pages, then stop early instead of continuing to hammer adjacent windows.
  5. Update the manifest after each attempt with timestamps, attempt counts, HTTP status, cache path, and error summary.
  6. Parse only cached success and empty windows into a flat table.
  7. Apply deterministic deduplication before writing the final Stage 1 CSV and Parquet outputs.

Should daily windows stay daily?

Important

The archived Zika RSS cache suggests that daily windows are safer than necessary for most days, but broader windows should still be kept modest.

Across 5,844 observed 1-day windows, the archive averaged 3.95 items per day with a median of 2. However, 7 days already reached 100 items, which likely reflects the practical Google News RSS ceiling on high-volume dates.

The best compromise from the retrospective simulation is 3-day windows. That setting would reduce requests by about 66.7% while keeping estimated cap-risk at 1.0%. In contrast, 7-day windows push cap-risk high enough to warrant caution, and 14-day+ windows look too aggressive for reliable historical retrieval.

Note

For the 3-day candidate, the archive contains 58 rolling windows where the summed daily counts exceed 100. These windows are then grouped into 12 broader covered spans when they overlap in calendar time.

The balance strategy would be 3-day -> 1-day -> back to 3-day retrieval logic, where the pipeline defaults to 3-day windows but falls back to daily windows if a 3-day window contains more than 100 items in the archive. This would allow for more efficient retrieval during quieter periods while still respecting the observed limits on busier days.

A hierarchical windows of 30-day -> 14-day-> 7-day -> 3-day -> 1-day can even be used!!!

Among the sample of 2,195 rows, there are 1812 rows where both models agree on the same label:

  • both models called irrelevant on 1022 rows (46.6% rows can be completely drop)
  • both models called relevant on 686 rows (31.3% of the total sample)
  • both models called unsure on 104 rows (4.7% of all paired rows)

Decision rule

  • drop if OpenAI = irrelevantand local = irrelevant (n=1022/1022).
  • keep if OpenAI = relevant and local = relevant and rationale_similarity >= 0.75. rationale_similarity is only computed when both models said relevant. It uses SBERT cosine similarity on the two rationales. Otherwise it is left as not applicable (n=614/686).
  • review for everything else. That means review covers:
    • any disagreement between models, (n=383)
    • any case where either model says unsure (n=104)
    • both say relevant but the rationale similarity is below threshold (n=72/686, with most rationale similarities above 0.7 and just below 0.75).
    • both say relevant but similarity could not be computed (n=0)

It is clearly seen that when OpenAI says irrelevant, the local model is often reluctant (just small percent-4% think that it is relevant). Instead, when OpenAI says unsure, the local model is only agree on 48.8% of the time, while the big difference is it thinks 32.9% of the case is relevant.

Investigating further showed that OpenAI tends to require a more explicit Zika signal in the headline, whereas the local model more often treats broader vector, surveillance, or outbreak context as relevant. Some examples where OpenAI==irrelevant but local==relevant|unsure:

Why some full-text retrievals failed

Step 3 failures are expected in a web-scale article-retrieval pipeline because the script is operating against publisher websites with heterogeneous access controls and HTML structures. A failed row does not necessarily mean that the URL resolution step failed; it often means the target publisher blocked automated access, returned too little extractable article text, or timed out before the extractor could finish.

For the current failed-output file:

  • 89 of 119 failed rows are direct HTTP 403 responses, which indicates that the target publisher accepted the request but refused to serve the article content to the scraper.
  • 15 rows resolved successfully but produced either too little article text or no usable extraction output after the fallback extractors ran.
  • 9 rows failed because the destination site timed out before the page could be fetched, and 1 row failed because of an SSL certificate verification problem.

The main interpretation is that Step 3 is constrained more by publisher access control and network variability than by the extraction code itself. In the current run, the single biggest source of failure is publisher blocking via HTTP 403, while the next tier of failures comes from pages that either timed out or yielded text that was too short to count as a usable article body.

Step 4 BERTopic on the retrieved full-text subset

To explore whether the retained full-text corpus contains coherent thematic structure beyond the headline labels, I first ran a standard BERTopic pipeline over the successful Stage 3 subset and then added an impact-guided BERTopic refinement. The modeling input is intentionally narrower than the raw zika_fulltext.csv table: the script keeps documents with non-empty text, enforces a minimum word-count threshold, applies a lightweight English-language filter, and truncates each document to a fixed word budget before embedding.

That refinement matters for interpretation. The fully unsupervised MiniLM baseline tended to collapse the retained corpus into very broad Zika-centered clusters, which is not especially useful when the research goal is to characterize impact pathways. The new impact-guided run therefore suppresses generic Zika vocabulary, seeds BERTopic with impact-oriented concept bundles, and uses a KMeans partition to force a more inspectable thematic split.

Following BERTopic’s modular design, the current report now treats the pipeline as six separate submodels:

  1. embeddings
  2. dimensionality reduction
  3. clustering
  4. vectorization
  5. c-TF-IDF weighting
  6. representation modeling

The generic zika_bertopic_* outputs correspond to the current baseline embedding backend, which remains all-MiniLM-L6-v2. The richer modular outputs are stored separately in zika_bertopic_modular_analysis.*, zika_bertopic_modular_topics.csv, and zika_bertopic_stage_timings.csv. The new impact-guided outputs are written to zika_bertopic_impact_*.

For the current impact-guided run, BERTopic received 496 successful full-text rows and modeled 488 documents after filtering. The full impact analysis took 7s, which splits into about 5.3 seconds for embedding generation, 1.3 seconds for BERTopic fitting, and 0.3 seconds for the 2D inspection layout.

Substantively, the impact-guided model is much closer to the research objective than the coarse unsupervised baseline. Instead of returning one dominant “general Zika” topic, it separates the retained corpus into interpretable impact pathways such as:

  • congenital outcomes and child risk
  • pregnancy and fetal neurodevelopment
  • vector ecology and climate risk
  • diagnostics and laboratory surveillance
  • travel advisories and regional surveillance
  • sexual and reproductive transmission
  • vaccines and therapeutics

This shift comes from three deliberate modeling choices: removing generic Zika vocabulary from the vectorizer, seeding the model with impact-oriented concept bundles, and using KMeans to force a finer topic partition. On the current corpus, those choices produce 8 non-outlier topics with no outlier bucket, and the largest topic accounts for only 25.0% of modeled documents. That is a much more useful structure for downstream impact screening than the earlier MiniLM baseline, where one topic dominated nearly the entire corpus.

The visual diagnostics help show why the new result is easier to investigate:

  • the topic-size chart shows that the retained full-text subset is no longer collapsing into one overwhelmingly generic theme
  • the 2D projection reveals distinct neighborhoods for reproductive transmission, diagnostics, travel/public-health alerts, and congenital outcomes
  • the yearly topic-mix figure makes it easier to see when certain impact pathways become more prevalent in the corpus

The earlier embedding and modular comparisons are still useful methodologically. They explain why the pipeline was refined in this direction:

  • Embedding comparison: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 remains faster and more stable than BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5, while BGE produces a more fragmented solution with 101 outliers.
  • Dimensionality reduction: UMAP is slower than PCA, but PCA still produces many outliers and a flatter, less interpretable structure.
  • Clustering: KMeans is the key reason the impact-guided run becomes granular enough to be useful. In the modular comparison it produces a finer partition than HDBSCAN on the same MiniLM embeddings.
  • Vectorizer, c-TF-IDF, and representation: these layers mostly affect topic wording, but once generic Zika words are suppressed they help surface more specific impact terms such as microcephaly, pregnancy, pcr, caribbean, and semen.

So the practical interpretation is:

  • the original unsupervised BERTopic baseline is still helpful as a methodological reference, but it is too generic for the impact-filtering objective
  • the new impact-guided BERTopic run is the more useful analytical output for this project because it organizes the retained Zika corpus into concrete impact pathways rather than repeating that the documents are about Zika
  • the inspection figures make it easier to decide which topics are worth keeping, merging, or refining further in later iterations
